subject: Architecture
title: The Roman Ponte Fabricio: Oldest Working Bridge
description: One-minute skill: The Roman Ponte Fabricio: Oldest Working Bridge.

hook.text: Rome's Ponte Fabricio was built in 62 BC and still carries pedestrians across the Tiber River today.

buildup.text: Its two stone arches span 187 feet, built from travertine and volcanic tufa by Lucius Fabricius.

discovery.text: An inscription on the bridge names the builder — rare proof of who designed an ancient Roman structure.

twist.text: The bridge survived floods, wars, and two millennia of use. Modern bridges often fail within 75 years.

climax.text: Roman bridge engineering spread across the empire — over 900 stone bridges were built in Europe alone.

punchline.text: A 2,000-year-old bridge. Still open. No maintenance budget needed.

quiz.question: When was the Ponte Fabricio built?

details.summary: The Ponte Fabricio in Rome, built in 62 BCE, is the oldest bridge in the world still in its original state and continuous use. Its two stone arches span the Tiber River connecting central Rome to Tiber Island, carrying pedestrian traffic for over 2,000 years without major reconstruction.
details.whyItMatters: A 2,000-year-old bridge still functioning daily proves that Roman engineering achieved durability modern construction rarely matches. The Ponte Fabricio challenges our throwaway approach to infrastructure with its multi-millennium service life.
takeaways: Built in 62 BCE — the world's oldest bridge still in original state
Two stone arches span the Tiber to Tiber Island
Over 2,000 years of continuous pedestrian use

faq.question: Why has the Ponte Fabricio lasted so long?
faq.answer: Roman builders used high-quality tufa and travertine stone, waterproof volcanic mortar, and a flood-relief opening between the arches that reduces water pressure during high water. Conservative over-engineering and excellent materials created a structure far stronger than necessary.

faq.question: How old is the second bridge to Tiber Island?
faq.answer: The Ponte Cestio on the island's other side was built around 46 BCE, though it was substantially rebuilt in the late 1800s. Unlike the Ponte Fabricio, which retains its original Roman structure, the Ponte Cestio is largely a modern reconstruction on ancient foundations.
